question: Dans le régime fédéral de protection des divulgateurs, à partir de quand calcule-t-on le délai pour porter plainte pour représailles?
model_answer:
Dans le régime fédéral de protection des divulgateurs, le délai pour porter plainte pour représailles commence à courir à partir du moment où le plaignant a connaissance des mesures de représailles ou des mesures proposées. Cela signifie que le calcul du délai débute lorsque le plaignant devient conscient des actions ou des décisions qui constituent des représailles à son égard, et non nécessairement à partir du moment où les représailles ont effectivement commencé ou ont été mises en œuvre.

Ce délai est généralement fixé par la législation ou les règlements spécifiques régissant la protection des divulgateurs dans le cadre fédéral. Par exemple, au Canada, sous la loi sur la protection des fonctionnaires divulgateurs d'actes répréhensibles, les fonctionnaires qui estiment avoir été victimes de représailles ont un certain délai, typiquement de 60 jours, pour déposer une plainte auprès du Tribunal de la dotation de la fonction publique. Ce délai peut varier en fonction des juridictions et des lois applicables.

Il est essentiel que les individus qui croient avoir subi des représailles pour avoir signalé des actes répréhensibles ou des irrégularités soient conscients de ces délais et suivent les procédures appropriées pour déposer leur plainte dans les temps. La consultation d'un avocat spécialisé en droit du travail ou en protection des divulgateurs peut s'avérer précieuse pour naviguer dans ces processus complexes et assurer que les droits du plaignant sont protégés.
reference_answer: Le délai ordinaire pour déposer une plainte de représailles auprès du Commissariat à l'intégrité du secteur public du Canada est de 60 jours à partir du jour où la personne savait, ou aurait dû savoir, qu'une mesure de représailles avait été prise. Le commissaire peut proroger ce délai selon les circonstances. La politique du 8 octobre 2026 précise que le simple fait de découvrir tardivement la loi ne suffit pas nécessairement à justifier une prolongation.
context_supporting_summary: Federal reprisal complaint ordinary time limit is 60 days from known/ought-to-have-known date. Commissioner may grant extension depending on circumstances; policy revised October 8 2026.
judge_reason: The answer correctly states that the 60‑day limitation begins when the complainant knows or ought to have known of the reprisals, matching the core rule. However, it misidentifies the appropriate adjudicating body (referring to the Tribunal de la dotation instead of the Commissioner of the Public Sector Integrity) and omits mention of possible extensions and the specific policy date, which are important conditions. These inaccuracies and omissions limit the practical usefulness of the guidance.

question: Can I view and print my SIN through My Service Canada Account?
model_answer:
According to the Government of Canada's website, you can view your Social Insurance Number (SIN) online through your My Service Canada Account (MSCA). However, you cannot print your SIN directly from your account.

To view your SIN online, follow these steps:

1. Sign in to your My Service Canada Account.
2. Click on "View my SIN" or "Social Insurance Number" from the dashboard.
3. Your SIN will be displayed on the screen.

If you need a paper copy of your SIN confirmation, you can request one through your MSCA account or by contacting Service Canada directly. They will mail a confirmation of your SIN to your address on file.

Please note that you should never share your SIN or print it on any document that may be accessible to others, as this can increase the risk of identity theft. It's essential to keep your SIN confidential and secure.
reference_answer: Yes. In My Service Canada Account, you can view and print your Social Insurance Number and check your name as recorded and any expiry date. Register or sign in, then open the 'Social Insurance Number' section. Your SIN is sensitive personal information, so protect copies and don't provide it when unnecessary.
context_supporting_summary: An eligible account holder can view and print their Social Insurance Number from MSCA. The dashboard also shows recorded names and any SIN expiry date; SIN remains sensitive personal information.
judge_reason: The answer correctly describes how to view the SIN in My Service Canada Account, but it incorrectly states that the SIN cannot be printed directly, contradicting the provided context that eligible users can view and print their SIN. This mis‑guidance on a core part of the question makes the response partially correct but substantially incomplete.

question: Si je retire de l’argent de mon CELI pendant que je suis non-résident, puis-je recotiser en franchise d’impôt sans redevenir résident?
model_answer:
En général, les règles fiscales entourant les comptes enregistrés, tels que les Comptes d'épargne libre d'impôt (CELI), peuvent varier en fonction de votre statut de résidence et des lois spécifiques de votre pays de résidence ou de citoyenneté. Pour répondre à votre question avec précision, il est essentiel de considérer les lois et réglementations fiscales du pays où vous êtes non-résident et celles du pays où vous avez ouvert votre CELI.

Généralement, les CELI sont conçus pour offrir des avantages fiscaux aux résidents du pays où ils sont offerts, permettant aux épargnants de gagner des intérêts ou des rendements sans payer d'impôt sur le revenu sur ces gains, sous certaines conditions. Cependant, lorsque vous devenez non-résident, votre statut fiscal change, et les règles qui s'appliquent à votre CELI peuvent également changer.

### Retirer de l'argent de votre CELI en tant que non-résident

- **Impôts**: En tant que non-résident, vous pourriez être soumis à des retenues d'impôt à la source sur les intérêts ou les gains en capital que vous retirez de votre CELI, selon les lois du pays où le compte est situé. Le traitement fiscal des retraits peut varier considérablement en fonction des accords fiscaux entre les pays.
  
- **Recotisation**: La capacité à recotiser (ou à réinvestir) des fonds dans un CELI en franchise d'impôt après les avoir retirés en tant que non-résident dépend des règles spécifiques du CELI et des lois fiscales du pays où le compte est situé. En général, les avantages fiscaux associés aux CELI sont conçus pour les résidents, et les contributions ou les recotisations peuvent être soumises à des restrictions ou à des conditions spécifiques pour les non-résidents.

### Recotiser sans redevenir résident

Il est peu probable que vous puissiez recotiser des fonds dans un CELI en franchise d'impôt sans redevenir résident, car les avantages fiscaux des CELI sont généralement réservés aux résidents. Cependant, cela peut dépendre des règles spécifiques du programme de CELI et des lois fiscales du pays où le compte est situé. Certains pays ou institutions financières peuvent offrir des options pour les non-résidents, mais ces options sont souvent soumises à des conditions et des restrictions spécifiques.

### Conseil

Étant donné la complexité des lois et réglementations fiscales, il est fortement recommandé de consulter un conseiller fiscal ou un professionnel de la finance qui est au courant des lois spécifiques de votre situation. Ils pourront vous fournir des conseils personnalisés sur la manière de gérer votre CELI en tant que non-résident, y compris les implications fiscales des retraits et les possibilités de recotiser des fonds.
reference_answer: Non. Un non-résident du Canada peut retirer de l'argent de son CELI sans impôt canadien sur le retrait, et ce retrait crée normalement des droits de cotisation à compter du 1er janvier suivant. Cependant, une cotisation effectuée alors que la personne est non-résidente est imposable, généralement à 1 % par mois tant qu'elle demeure dans le compte, même s'il existe des droits inutilisés. Il faut attendre d'être redevenu résident pour cotiser à nouveau en franchise d'impôt.

A TFSA contribution made while non-resident is generally subject to 1% monthly tax, even where unused contribution room is available; exception for qualifying transfers.

It also adds unnecessary foreign‑tax speculation. Thus it applies Canadian knowledge partially but is incomplete.

question: What is the difference between a property assessment and a property tax bill in the Northwest Territories?
model_answer:
In the Northwest Territories (NWT), Canada, a property assessment and a property tax bill are two related but distinct concepts. Here's a breakdown of the difference:

**Property Assessment:**
A property assessment is an estimate of a property's market value, which is used as a basis for calculating property taxes. In the NWT, property assessments are conducted by the Department of Municipal and Community Affairs (MACA) or by a designated assessment authority. The assessment takes into account factors such as:

* Property size and location
* Type of property (residential, commercial, industrial, etc.)
* Age and condition of the property
* Recent sales of similar properties in the area

The assessed value is usually expressed as a percentage of the property's market value, which is then used to calculate the property taxes.

**Property Tax Bill:**
A property tax bill, on the other hand, is the actual amount of taxes owed on a property, based on the assessed value. The property tax bill is calculated by multiplying the assessed value by the tax rate set by the municipal government or the territorial government.

In the NWT, property tax bills are typically issued annually and are payable to the municipal government or the territorial government, depending on the location of the property. The tax bill will include information such as:

* Assessed value of the property
* Tax rate
* Total taxes owed
* Payment due dates

Key differences:

* A property assessment is an estimate of a property's value, while a property tax bill is the actual amount of taxes owed.
* A property assessment is used to determine the taxable value of a property, while a property tax bill is the result of applying the tax rate to the assessed value.

To illustrate the difference, consider an example:

* A residential property in Yellowknife is assessed at $400,000 (100% of its market value).
* The municipal tax rate is 1.25% of the assessed value.
* The property tax bill would be $5,000 (1.25% of $400,000).

In this example, the property assessment is $400,000, and the property tax bill is $5,000.

question: What is the difference between a property assessment and a property tax bill in the Northwest Territories?
model_answer:
In the Northwest Territories (NWT), Canada, a property assessment and a property tax bill are two related but distinct concepts. Here's a breakdown of the difference:

**Property Assessment:**
A property assessment is an estimate of a property's market value, which is used as a basis for calculating property taxes. In the NWT, property assessments are conducted by the Department of Municipal and Community Affairs (MACA) or by a designated assessment authority. The assessment takes into account factors such as:

* Property size and location
* Type of property (residential, commercial, industrial, etc.)
* Age and condition of the property
* Recent sales of similar properties in the area

The assessed value is usually expressed as a percentage of the property's market value, which is then used to calculate the property taxes.

**Property Tax Bill:**
A property tax bill, on the other hand, is the actual amount of taxes owed on a property, based on the assessed value. The property tax bill is calculated by multiplying the assessed value by the tax rate set by the municipal government or the territorial government.

In the NWT, property tax bills are typically issued annually and are payable to the municipal government or the territorial government, depending on the location of the property. The tax bill will include information such as:

* Assessed value of the property
* Tax rate
* Total taxes owed
* Payment due dates

Key differences:

* A property assessment is an estimate of a property's value, while a property tax bill is the actual amount of taxes owed.
* A property assessment is used to determine the taxable value of a property, while a property tax bill is the result of applying the tax rate to the assessed value.

To illustrate the difference, consider an example:

* A residential property in Yellowknife is assessed at $400,000 (100% of its market value).
* The municipal tax rate is 1.25% of the assessed value.
* The property tax bill would be $5,000 (1.25% of $400,000).

In this example, the property assessment is $400,000, and the property tax bill is $5,000.

question: Who has to show that an electronic document is authentic when it’s offered as evidence under the Canada Evidence Act?
model_answer:
Under the Canada Evidence Act, the party who is offering the electronic document as evidence has the burden of proving its authenticity. This means that the party who is introducing the electronic document into evidence must show that it is what they claim it is, and that it has not been altered or tampered with in any way.

Section 31.2 of the Canada Evidence Act states that "a person seeking to prove the authenticity of an electronic document must provide evidence of its authenticity, in the absence of which the document is not admissible". This places the onus on the party offering the electronic document to provide sufficient evidence to establish its authenticity.

This can involve providing evidence about the origin of the document, its creation and storage, and any measures taken to ensure its integrity and security. The party may also need to call witnesses or provide expert testimony to support the authenticity of the document.

It's worth noting that the Canada Evidence Act also provides some presumptions of authenticity for certain types of electronic documents, such as electronic records that are kept in the ordinary course of business. However, these presumptions can be rebutted by the opposing party, and the party offering the document still has the ultimate burden of proving its authenticity.
reference_answer: The party seeking to admit the electronic document as evidence must prove its authenticity, by offering evidence capable of supporting a finding that the document is what the party claims it to be. Section 31.1 of the Canada Evidence Act places that burden on the proponent; this authentication requirement is distinct from the Act's separate best-evidence rule for electronic records.

question: Puis-je renoncer à ma citoyenneté canadienne si cela me rend apatride?
model_answer:
En général, la loi canadienne sur la citoyenneté permet aux citoyens canadiens de renoncer à leur citoyenneté, mais cela est soumis à certaines conditions et exceptions. Selon la Loi sur la citoyenneté, un citoyen canadien peut renoncer à sa citoyenneté par déclaration, mais uniquement s'il possède une autre citoyenneté ou s'il a une demande de citoyenneté en cours ailleurs.

Cependant, si vous renoncez à la citoyenneté canadienne et que vous ne possédez pas une autre citoyenneté, vous pouvez devenir apatride. La loi canadienne sur la citoyenneté vise à éviter les situations dans lesquelles une personne deviendrait apatride à la suite de la perte de la citoyenneté canadienne.

Si vous envisagez de renoncer à la citoyenneté canadienne, il est essentiel de consulter un avocat spécialisé en droit de la citoyenneté ou de contacter le gouvernement canadien pour obtenir des conseils sur les conséquences potentielles et les exigences pour renoncer à la citoyenneté. Ils peuvent vous aider à comprendre vos options et à vous assurer que vous ne deviendrez pas apatride.

En outre, il convient de noter que devenir apatride peut avoir des conséquences importantes, notamment des difficultés à voyager, à travailler ou à accéder à des services essentiels. Il est donc crucial de bien peser les avantages et les inconvénients potentiels avant de prendre une décision.
reference_answer: Non, pas selon la procédure ordinaire de renonciation prévue à l'article 9 de la Loi sur la citoyenneté. Vous devez déjà posséder une autre nationalité ou l'acquérir si votre demande est acceptée, afin de ne pas devenir apatride par cette renonciation. Le ministre peut dispenser de certaines autres conditions pour motifs d'ordre humanitaire, mais cette dispense ne s'étend pas à l'exigence d'une autre nationalité.
context_supporting_summary: Under s9(1)(a), a renouncing Canadian must already possess another country's citizenship or become one upon acceptance. Humanitarian ministerial discretion in s9(2) waives only s9(1)(d) or (e); it cannot waive other nationality requirement (a).
judge_reason: The answer mentions that renunciation is possible only with another citizenship or a pending application, but the reference only requires an existing other citizenship (or acquiring one upon acceptance) and does not support the claim about a pending application. It also fails to state the key rule that one cannot renounce if it would render them stateless, and omits the detail that humanitarian discretion cannot waive the nationality requirement. While it correctly notes that the law seeks to avoid statelessness, the inaccurate condition and missing mandatory prohibition constitute major factual omissions.

question: Can I vouch for several neighbours who lack ID in a federal election?
model_answer:
In a federal election, voters are typically required to provide identification to verify their identity and eligibility to vote. The specific rules and requirements for voter identification can vary depending on the country, state, or province where the election is taking place.

In Canada, for example, voters can use one of the accepted pieces of identification to prove their identity and address. If a voter lacks the required identification, they can take an oath and have another voter who knows them and is entitled to vote in the same polling division vouch for their identity.

However, the rules regarding vouching can be specific. For instance, in Canadian federal elections, a voter can vouch for only one person, and the person vouching must also meet the identification requirements. Additionally, both the voter and the person vouching must take an oath and sign a document.

To provide accurate and up-to-date information, I recommend checking with the relevant electoral authority in your country or region for the most current rules and regulations regarding voter identification and vouching procedures. They can provide detailed guidance on what forms of identification are accepted, under what circumstances vouching is allowed, and any specific requirements or limitations that apply.
reference_answer: Generally no. Under the Canada Elections Act, a voter may normally vouch for the identity and address of only one other person in a federal election. There are limited exceptions, such as qualified employees assisting residents of seniors' residences or long-term care facilities, subject to specific rules. A person cannot vouch for several neighbours merely because they know them.
context_supporting_summary: One eligible elector can ordinarily vouch for identity/address of only one other elector per election. An eligible employee of seniors residence or long-term care facility can vouch for more than one resident under special conditions.
judge_reason: The answer correctly identifies the Canadian federal election context and applies the Canada Elections Act rule that a voter may vouch for only one other person, which directly answers the user’s scenario. It provides appropriate reasoning and practical guidance to verify with authorities. The only shortcoming is the omission of the limited exception for employees of seniors residences, a detail present in the reference but not essential for the neighbour scenario, so the guidance is still essentially correct.

question: Un ministère fédéral doit-il toujours refuser de communiquer des renseignements personnels dans une réponse d’accès à l’information?
model_answer:
Non, un ministère fédéral n’est pas toujours obligé de refuser de communiquer des renseignements personnels dans une réponse d’accès à l’information. Cependant, les ministères fédéraux sont soumis à la Loi sur l'accès à l'information (LAI) et à la Loi sur la protection des renseignements personnels (LPRP), qui régissent la gestion des renseignements personnels et l'accès à l'information.

Lorsqu'une demande d'accès à l'information est faite en vertu de la LAI, le ministère fédéral doit évaluer si les documents demandés contiennent des renseignements personnels au sens de la LPRP. Si c'est le cas, le ministère doit appliquer les exceptions et les exemptions prévues dans la LPRP pour déterminer si ces renseignements peuvent être communiqués.

Selon la LPRP, les renseignements personnels ne peuvent être communiqués sans le consentement de l'individu concerné que dans certaines circonstances, telles que :

1. **Si la loi l'exige** : Si une autre loi fédérale exige la communication de ces renseignements.
2. **Pour l'exécution d'un programme ou d'une activité** : Si la communication est nécessaire pour l'exécution d'un programme ou d'une activité du ministère.
3. **Pour des fins de recherche ou de statistique** : Sous certaines conditions, les renseignements personnels peuvent être communiqués pour des fins de recherche ou de statistique, mais des mesures doivent être prises pour protéger l'identité des individus.
4. **Dans des situations d'urgence** : Si la communication est nécessaire pour prévenir des dommages graves ou immédiats à la santé ou à la sécurité de l'individu ou d'autrui.

Avant de communiquer des renseignements personnels, le ministère fédéral doit s'assurer qu'il respecte les dispositions de la LPRP et qu'il a le droit de divulguer ces informations. Dans de nombreux cas, les ministères peuvent avoir recours à la technique du "refus partielle", où les parties des documents qui contiennent des renseignements personnels sont caviardées (masquées) avant leur communication, afin de protéger la vie privée des individus tout en fournissant autant d'information que possible en réponse à la demande d'accès.

En résumé, bien que les ministères fédéraux aient l'obligation de protéger les renseignements personnels, ils ne sont pas toujours obligés de refuser de communiquer ces renseignements dans une réponse d'accès à l'information. La décision de communiquer ou non ces renseignements dépend de l'application des dispositions spécifiques de la LPRP et de la LAI.
reference_answer: Non. L'article 19(1) de la Loi sur l'accès à l'information exige en principe de refuser la divulgation des renseignements personnels. Toutefois, le paragraphe 19(2) autorise une communication si la personne concernée consent, si les renseignements sont déjà accessibles au public ou si l'article 8 de la Loi sur la protection des renseignements personnels le permet. Il faut vérifier que l'une de ces exceptions s'applique réellement.

This constitutes a material jurisdictional error despite recognizing the relevant institutions.

question: Who hears an appeal if an Ontario municipality refuses my request for municipal records?

To appeal a municipality's decision, you would need to submit a formal appeal to the IPC within 30 days of receiving the municipality's decision. The IPC will then review the appeal and may request additional information or evidence from both you and the municipality.

question: Après six mois de travail continu dans un emploi assujetti au régime fédéral, puis-je demander un changement de lieu de travail?
model_answer:
En général, les règles concernant les demandes de changement de lieu de travail (ou de mutation) peuvent varier en fonction de l'entreprise, du secteur d'activité et des lois du pays ou de la région où vous travaillez. Cependant, je peux vous fournir des informations générales qui pourraient s'appliquer à votre situation.

Dans de nombreux cas, les employés qui souhaitent demander un changement de lieu de travail après six mois de travail continu dans un emploi assujetti au régime fédéral (comme aux États-Unis, par exemple) peuvent le faire, mais cela dépend de plusieurs facteurs :

1. **Politique de l'entreprise** : Chaque entreprise a ses propres règles et procédures concernant les demandes de changement de lieu de travail. Certaines entreprises peuvent avoir des politiques plus flexibles que d'autres. Il est essentiel de consulter votre contrat de travail ou de discuter avec le département des ressources humaines (RH) pour comprendre les politiques spécifiques de votre employeur.

2. **Performance et ancienneté** : Généralement, les employés qui ont une bonne performance et une certaine ancienneté dans l'entreprise sont plus susceptibles de voir leur demande de changement de lieu de travail acceptée. Six mois peuvent être considérés comme une période relativement courte, mais si vous avez démontré votre valeur pour l'entreprise et que vous avez des raisons valables pour demander un changement, cela pourrait être pris en compte.

3. **Disponibilité des postes** : Le changement de lieu de travail dépend souvent de la disponibilité des postes dans le nouveau lieu que vous avez choisi. Si il n'y a pas de poste disponible qui correspond à vos compétences et à votre expérience, il pourrait être plus difficile d'obtenir un changement de lieu de travail.

4. **Raisons de la demande** : Les raisons behind votre demande de changement de lieu de travail peuvent également jouer un rôle. Les raisons personnelles, familiales ou de santé sont souvent considérées plus sympathiquement que les raisons purement préférentielles.

Avant de demander un changement de lieu de travail, il est conseillé de :

- **Discuter avec votre supérieur ou le département RH** : Pour comprendre les possibilités et les procédures à suivre.
- **Évaluer vos performances** : Assurez-vous d'avoir une bonne performance et d'être considéré comme un employé valeureux.
- **Préparer vos raisons** : Soyez prêt à expliquer clairement pourquoi vous souhaitez un changement de lieu de travail et comment cela pourrait bénéficier à la fois à vous et à l'entreprise.

Gardez à l'esprit que chaque situation est unique, et les règles spécifiques à votre cas dépendront de votre employeur et des lois applicables dans votre juridiction.
reference_answer: Oui. Après six mois consécutifs de service continu auprès d'un employeur de compétence fédérale, vous pouvez demander par écrit une modification de votre lieu de travail en vertu de l'article 177.1 du Code canadien du travail. La demande doit préciser notamment la modification et les dates souhaitées. L'employeur doit y répondre suivant le Code, mais il peut refuser pour certains motifs légaux; le droit de demander n'est pas une garantie d'obtenir le changement.

question: If both official languages are chosen by the parties in a federal court proceeding, can the judge rely on an interpreter to understand one of them?
model_answer:
In Canada, both English and French are official languages, and parties have the right to use either language in federal court proceedings. If both languages are chosen by the parties, the court must ensure that the proceedings are conducted in a way that respects the language rights of all parties.

According to the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms and the Federal Courts Rules, if a party chooses to use one of the official languages, the court must provide interpretation services to ensure that the judge, the other parties, and the court staff can understand the language being used.

In this scenario, if both official languages are chosen by the parties, the judge may rely on an interpreter to understand one of the languages, but only to the extent necessary to ensure that the judge can understand the evidence and arguments being presented.

The judge is still required to be proficient in one of the official languages, but may use interpretation services to facilitate their understanding of the other language. The interpreter's role is to provide a simultaneous or consecutive interpretation of the evidence and arguments being presented, allowing the judge to follow the proceedings and make informed decisions.

It's worth noting that the use of interpretation services in federal court proceedings is governed by the Federal Courts Rules and the Interpretation Act, which set out the rules and procedures for the use of interpreters in court. The court must also ensure that the interpreter is qualified and impartial, and that the interpretation services provided are accurate and reliable.
reference_answer: No, not for understanding the evidence and arguments in the chosen official languages. Under section 16(1)(c) of the federal Official Languages Act, if the parties choose both English and French in proceedings before a federal court, the court must ensure that every judge or other officer hearing the case understands both languages without an interpreter. The requirement concerns the court's adjudicative functions, not every employee or every courtroom service.
context_supporting_summary: When both French and English chosen by federal-court parties, judge or other hearing officer must understand both without interpreter. The bilingual-competence duty applies to adjudicative functions and is not equivalent to banning all court interpretation services.
judge_reason: The answer identifies the federal court and language rights but misstates the core duty: it says a judge may rely on an interpreter, whereas the Official Languages Act requires the adjudicating judge to understand both languages without one. This material misattribution of responsibility shows an important jurisdictional error despite recognizing the correct institutions.

question: Who is responsible for managing a federally incorporated business corporation’s affairs?
model_answer:
In a federally incorporated business corporation in Canada, the affairs of the corporation are managed by its board of directors. The board of directors is responsible for making major decisions regarding the corporation's business and affairs, and for overseeing the management of the corporation.

The board of directors is typically composed of individuals elected by the corporation's shareholders, and may include both executive directors (who are also officers of the corporation) and non-executive directors (who are not involved in the day-to-day management of the corporation).

Some of the key responsibilities of the board of directors include:

* Setting the corporation's overall strategy and direction
* Approving major business decisions, such as mergers and acquisitions, investments, and financings
* Overseeing the management of the corporation, including the appointment and removal of officers
* Reviewing and approving financial statements and budgets
* Ensuring compliance with applicable laws and regulations

The board of directors may also delegate certain responsibilities to committees, such as an audit committee or a compensation committee, to assist with specific aspects of the corporation's management.

It's worth noting that the Canada Business Corporations Act (CBCA) sets out the framework for the governance of federally incorporated business corporations in Canada, and provides rules and guidelines for the management of these corporations.
reference_answer: Under section 102(1) of the Canada Business Corporations Act, the board of directors manages or supervises management of the business and affairs of a federally incorporated business corporation. A unanimous shareholder agreement may restrict the directors' authority and transfer specified decision-making powers. The directors' governance role should not be confused with management's day-to-day operations.
context_supporting_summary: Board of directors manages or supervises management of federally incorporated company's business and affairs. The management duty is explicitly subject to unanimous shareholders' agreement, which can restrict director powers.
judge_reason: The answer correctly identifies the board of directors as the body that manages or supervises the affairs of a federally incorporated corporation, cites the Canada Business Corporations Act, and outlines the board's key responsibilities, matching the core institutional role. It omits the nuance about a unanimous shareholder agreement potentially restricting director authority, but this is a minor omission rather than a material error.

question: Au Québec, les frais de dépôt aux petites créances sont-ils les mêmes pour un particulier et une société?

question: Can bankruptcy discharge a government student loan if I stopped being a student only three years ago?
model_answer:
Generally, government student loans are not dischargeable in bankruptcy unless you can prove "undue hardship," which is a high standard to meet. The fact that you stopped being a student only three years ago may make it even more challenging to discharge your student loan debt.

In the United States, the Bankruptcy Code (11 U.S.C. § 523(a)(8)) makes student loans non-dischargeable unless the borrower can demonstrate that repayment would impose an "undue hardship" on them or their dependents. To determine undue hardship, courts often apply the Brunner test, which requires you to show:

1. **You cannot maintain a minimal standard of living** for yourself and your dependents if forced to repay the loan.
2. **Your financial situation is likely to persist** for a significant portion of the repayment period.
3. **You have made good faith efforts** to repay the loan before seeking bankruptcy.

Given that you stopped being a student only three years ago, it may be difficult to argue that you've made good faith efforts to repay the loan or that your financial situation is likely to persist for a significant portion of the repayment period.

That being said, it's not impossible to discharge a government student loan in bankruptcy, even if you're only three years out of school. If you can demonstrate extraordinary circumstances, such as a serious medical condition, a disability, or another significant hardship, you may still be able to make a case for undue hardship.

To explore your options, I recommend consulting with a qualified bankruptcy attorney who can assess your individual circumstances and provide guidance on the best course of action. They can help you determine whether pursuing a bankruptcy discharge or other alternatives, such as income-driven repayment plans or loan forgiveness programs, might be more suitable for your situation.

Keep in mind that bankruptcy laws and regulations can be complex, and the specifics of your case will play a significant role in determining the outcome. A knowledgeable attorney can help you navigate the process and make informed decisions about your student loan debt.
reference_answer: Ordinarily no. Under section 178(1)(g) of the Bankruptcy and Insolvency Act, a qualifying federal or provincial student loan is not discharged if bankruptcy occurs while the borrower is still a student or within seven years after they cease to be a full- or part-time student. After five years, a court may grant hardship relief if the borrower has acted in good faith and will continue to experience financial difficulty that prevents repayment. At three years, that hardship exception is not yet available.

Court can grant hardship relief from student-loan exception after five years if good faith and ongoing financial inability; not after three.

question: En combien de temps un importateur doit-il transmettre les renseignements dont il dispose sur un incident lié à un produit de consommation?
model_answer: Un importateur doit transmettre les renseignements dont il dispose sur un incident lié à un produit de consommation dans les 2 jours ouvrables.
reference_answer: En vertu de l'article 14(2) de la Loi canadienne sur la sécurité des produits de consommation, une personne qui importe un produit de consommation à des fins commerciales et qui prend connaissance d'un incident visé par la loi doit fournir au ministre et, le cas échéant, au fournisseur les renseignements en sa possession dans les deux jours suivant le jour où elle en prend connaissance. Si le fabricant est établi à l'extérieur du Canada, l'importateur doit en outre présenter au ministre le rapport écrit prévu au paragraphe 14(3) dans les dix jours suivant cette prise de connaissance, sauf délai différent précisé par le ministre.
context_supporting_summary: Importers must send information in their control to Minister and original supplier within two days after awareness of reportable incident. When manufacturer outside Canada, importer must also file written report within ten days, unless Minister specifies another period.
judge_reason: The answer correctly states the two‑day reporting requirement under the Consumer Product Safety Act, but it omits the additional ten‑day written report obligation when the manufacturer is outside Canada, which is a key condition mentioned in the expected answer and context. Thus it provides partially workable guidance while overlooking an important condition.

question: What does the Canada National Parks Act say should come first when the minister manages a national park?
model_answer:
According to the Canada National Parks Act, when managing a national park, the Minister must prioritize the following:

"...the maintenance of ecological integrity, through the protection of natural resources and natural processes, shall be the first priority when considering all aspects of the management of parks."

This means that the Minister's primary consideration when making decisions about national park management should be to maintain the ecological integrity of the park, which involves protecting the park's natural resources and natural processes.

Source: Section 8(2) of the Canada National Parks Act (S.C. 2000, c. 32)

Under section 8(2) of the Canada National Parks Act, this means putting protection of natural resources and natural processes first, while making park-use and visitor decisions within that framework. It does not make recreation or heritage education irrelevant; they must be considered consistently with that statutory priority.

question: Une crise qui dépasse les capacités d’une province est-elle automatiquement une urgence nationale au sens de la Loi sur les mesures d’urgence?
model_answer: Non, une crise qui dépasse les capacités d’une province n’est pas automatiquement une urgence nationale au sens de la Loi sur les mesures d’urgence. La déclaration d’une urgence nationale nécessite une évaluation et une déclaration formelle par le gouvernement fédéral, conformément aux critères et aux procédures établis par la loi.
reference_answer: Non. Le fait qu'une situation dépasse les capacités d'une province ne suffit pas, à lui seul, à satisfaire à la définition d'« urgence nationale » de l'article 3 de la Loi sur les mesures d'urgence. Il faut une situation temporaire, urgente et critique qui, soit menace gravement la vie, la santé ou la sécurité des Canadiens et dépasse les capacités ou compétences d'une province, soit menace gravement la souveraineté, la sécurité ou l'intégrité territoriale du Canada. Dans les deux cas, aucune autre loi fédérale ne doit permettre d'y faire face efficacement.
context_supporting_summary: A national emergency must be urgent, critical and temporary and meet danger to Canadians beyond a province's capacity/authority or serious sovereignty/security threat. In either case, it must be a situation not effectively addressable under any other Canadian law; provincial capacity alone is insufficient.
judge_reason: The answer correctly states that a crisis exceeding a province's capacity does not automatically trigger a national emergency and that a formal federal declaration is required, which aligns with the supplied context. It does not introduce any unsupported or fabricated claims. The response omits the detailed criteria (temporariness, urgency, criticality, threat to life or sovereignty, and lack of other legislative solutions) that the reference includes, but this omission is a minor completeness issue rather than a factual error.

question: How long does Manitoba health coverage generally continue after I permanently move to another Canadian province?
model_answer:
In Manitoba, Canada, when you permanently move to another province, your Manitoba health coverage will generally continue for a limited time. According to the Manitoba government's website, you will typically remain covered under the Manitoba Health, Seniors and Active Living (MHSAL) plan for a period of 3 months after you leave the province, provided you have notified them of your move.

However, it's essential to note that this 3-month extension is subject to certain conditions. You must:

1. Notify MHSAL in writing, informing them of your permanent move to another province.
2. Provide proof of your new address and residency in the other province.

During this 3-month period, you will still be eligible for insured health services in Manitoba, but you may need to pay out-of-pocket for services received in your new province. It's crucial to apply for health coverage in your new province as soon as possible to avoid any gaps in coverage.

After the 3-month period, your Manitoba health coverage will terminate, and you will no longer be eligible for benefits under the MHSAL plan. At that point, you will need to rely on your new province's health plan for coverage.

To ensure a smooth transition, it's recommended that you:

* Notify MHSAL of your move as soon as possible.
* Apply for health coverage in your new province.
* Familiarize yourself with the health care system and coverage in your new province.

Keep in mind that health care coverage and regulations can vary between provinces, so it's essential to understand the specifics of your new province's health plan to avoid any unexpected costs or gaps in coverage.
reference_answer: When an ordinarily eligible Manitoba resident permanently moves to another province or territory, Manitoba health coverage generally continues for the rest of the month of arrival there and the following two months. Apply promptly to the new province's health plan to avoid a gap. Important exception: Manitoba says its coverage for a temporary foreign worker ends on the day the worker leaves Manitoba, so the general two-month extension should not be presented as universal.
context_supporting_summary: Manitoba ordinary eligible coverage persists for remainder of move month and next two months after permanent move. Exception: Manitoba temporary foreign worker coverage stops the day worker leaves Manitoba.
judge_reason: The answer gives a generally correct process (notify MHSAL, apply in new province) but states the coverage period as a flat three months, which contradicts the Canadian rule that coverage lasts only for the remainder of the arrival month plus the next two months. It also omits the noted exception for temporary foreign workers. Because the core factual detail is wrong, the guidance is substantially inaccurate, placing it in the low‑mid range.

question: Si je refuse l’assurance dentaire offerte par mon employeur, est-ce que je peux répondre que je n’y ai pas accès pour le régime dentaire canadien?
model_answer:
Si vous refusez l'assurance dentaire offerte par votre employeur, cela ne signifie pas automatiquement que vous n'avez pas accès à un régime dentaire. Cependant, pour déterminer si vous pouvez prétendre à un régime dentaire canadien spécifique, il est essentiel de comprendre les critères d'admissibilité pour ce régime.

Au Canada, les régimes dentaires sont souvent offerts par les employeurs comme avantages sociaux, mais il existe également des régimes dentaires privés que les individus peuvent acheter. Si vous refusez l'assurance dentaire offerte par votre employeur, vous pourriez toujours être admissible à d'autres régimes dentaires, qu'il s'agisse de plans privés ou, dans certains cas, de programmes gouvernementaux si vous remplissez leurs critères d'admissibilité.

Pour répondre à votre question de manière plus précise :

1. **Régimes dentaires privés** : Vous pouvez toujours souscrire un régime dentaire privé en dehors de celui offert par votre employeur. Ces régimes peuvent varier en termes de couverture, de coûts et d'exclusions, mais ils sont généralement accessibles à quiconque est prêt à payer les primes.

question: Does being approved for the disability tax credit automatically make me eligible for the Canada Disability Benefit?
model_answer:
Being approved for the Disability Tax Credit (DTC) does not automatically make you eligible for the Canada Disability Benefit. While the DTC is a federal tax credit for individuals with disabilities, the Canada Disability Benefit is a separate program with its own eligibility criteria.

The Canada Disability Benefit is a new benefit that was introduced in 2021, and it provides a monthly payment to eligible Canadians with disabilities. To be eligible for the Canada Disability Benefit, you must meet certain criteria, including:

1. Being a Canadian citizen, permanent resident, or protected person
2. Being at least 18 years old
3. Having a disability that is severe and prolonged, as defined by the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA)
4. Having a net income below a certain threshold (currently $28,809 for a single person or $37,789 for a couple)
5. Not being eligible for the Quebec Disability Benefit (if you live in Quebec)

Having a DTC approval can be helpful in supporting your application for the Canada Disability Benefit, as it may be considered as part of the eligibility assessment. However, it is not a guarantee of eligibility, and you will need to apply separately for the Canada Disability Benefit and meet the specific eligibility criteria.

It's recommended that you contact the CRA or a qualified benefits advisor to determine your eligibility for the Canada Disability Benefit and to get guidance on the application process.
reference_answer: No. Disability Tax Credit approval is necessary but not sufficient to receive the Canada Disability Benefit. You must also normally be aged 18–64, be a Canadian resident for income-tax purposes, have an eligible citizenship or immigration status, and ensure that you and your spouse or partner, if applicable, filed the required federal tax returns. For payments based on the rules posted in September 2026, the government requires 2025 returns. Eligibility may also depend on incarceration status.
context_supporting_summary: Disability Tax Credit is necessary but not sufficient for Canada Disability Benefit eligibility. 2026 rules also require age, residence, status, 2025 tax filing and other conditions.
judge_reason: The answer correctly states that DTC approval alone does not guarantee Canada Disability Benefit eligibility and lists several core criteria (citizenship/residency, minimum age, income threshold). However, it omits key conditions mentioned in the context such as the upper age limit (typically 64), the requirement to have filed the 2025 tax returns, and other nuances like incarceration status. These missing but material eligibility factors mean the guidance is only partially complete.

question: Could a withdrawal from my RDSP make me repay more in government grants or bonds than I actually withdraw?
model_answer:
Yes, it is possible for a withdrawal from a Registered Disability Savings Plan (RDSP) to trigger a repayment of more in government grants or bonds than the amount you actually withdraw. This is due to the way RDSPs are designed and the rules surrounding the repayment of government contributions.

In Canada, RDSPs are savings plans designed for individuals with severe and prolonged disabilities. The government incentivizes savings by contributing grants and bonds to the plan based on contributions made by the beneficiary or their family members. The Canada Disability Savings Grant (CDSG) and the Canada Disability Savings Bond (CDSB) are the two types of government contributions.

1. **Canada Disability Savings Grant (CDSG):** The CDSG is a matching grant based on the contributions made to the RDSP. The government matches contributions up to a certain percentage, and there is a lifetime limit on how much grant an individual can receive.

2. **Canada Disability Savings Bond (CDSB):** The CDSB is a direct contribution from the government into an RDSP for low-income and modest-income families. It does not require any contributions to be made to the RDSP to be eligible.

The key aspect to consider is the "Assistance Holdback Amount" (AHA), which is a critical component in understanding how withdrawals can affect government contributions. When you withdraw funds from an RDSP, you may be required to repay some or all of the government grants and bonds received in the 10 years preceding the withdrawal. This repayment is known as the Assistance Holdback Amount.

- **Calculation of Assistance Holdback Amount (AHA):** The AHA is calculated based on the total amount of CDSG and CDSB received in the 10 years before the withdrawal, minus any previous repayments. If the total amount of government contributions in the last 10 years exceeds the amount you are withdrawing, you could end up repaying more in grants or bonds than the amount you withdraw.

- **Example:** Suppose in the last 10 years, your RDSP received $10,000 in CDSG and $1,500 in CDSB, totaling $11,500 in government contributions. If you then decide to withdraw $5,000 from your RDSP, you might have to repay the full $11,500 if that's the Assistance Holdback Amount at the time of withdrawal, even though you're only taking out $5,000. However, the actual repayment would depend on the specific circumstances and the RDSP's balance.

It's essential to carefully consider the potential impact of withdrawals on government contributions before taking out funds from an RDSP. Consulting with a financial advisor who is knowledgeable about RDSPs and their intricacies can provide personalized guidance tailored to your specific situation. They can help you navigate the complexities and make informed decisions about your RDSP withdrawals.
reference_answer: Yes, for many withdrawals before age 60. Under the registered disability savings plan's proportional repayment rule, withdrawing $1 can require repaying $3 in recent Canada Disability Savings Grants and Bonds, up to the plan's assistance holdback amount. The rule has important exceptions and changes, including ordinary withdrawals in or after the year the beneficiary turns 60 and certain situations following loss of Disability Tax Credit eligibility. The exact repayment depends on the plan's recent grants and bonds.
context_supporting_summary: Each $1 withdrawn from RDSP can trigger $3 repayment of recent grant/bond funds up to holdback amount. Rules include conditions and exceptions, so exact repayment not universally $3 per dollar.
judge_reason: The answer recognises that RDSP withdrawals can trigger repayment of government grants and bonds and mentions the assistance hold‑back amount, showing some relevant Canadian knowledge. However it misstates how the hold‑back works—suggesting you might have to repay the full amount of grants received in the past ten years, which is inaccurate—and omits key conditions such as the 3‑to‑1 proportional repayment rule, the age‑60 exception, and other specific exceptions. Because it applies the concept but with incorrect calculations and missing important rules, it falls into the partially workable range.

question: Au Nouveau-Brunswick, puis-je faire transférer mon dépôt de garantie au nouveau locataire qui reprend mon bail?
model_answer:
Oui, au Nouveau-Brunswick, il est possible de transférer votre dépôt de garantie au nouveau locataire qui reprend votre bail, mais cela doit être fait avec l'accord du propriétaire. Voici les étapes à suivre :

1. **Obtenez l'accord du propriétaire** : Avant de transférer votre dépôt de garantie, vous devez obtenir l'accord écrit du propriétaire. Il est essentiel de communiquer clairement avec lui pour s'assurer qu'il est d'accord avec le transfert.
2. **Trouvez un nouveau locataire** : Vous devez trouver un nouveau locataire qui accepte de reprendre votre bail et de prendre en charge les responsabilités qui y sont liées.
3. **Rédigez un accord de transfert** : Vous, le nouveau locataire et le propriétaire devez rédiger un accord de transfert qui précise les conditions du transfert de dépôt de garantie. Cet accord doit inclure les détails suivants :
 * Le montant du dépôt de garantie à transférer
 * Les conditions de reprise du bail par le nouveau locataire
 * Les responsabilités du nouveau locataire en ce qui concerne le dépôt de garantie
4. **Signez l'accord de transfert** : Une fois que l'accord de transfert est rédigé, vous, le nouveau locataire et le propriétaire devez le signer. Cela officialise le transfert de dépôt de garantie.
5. **Mettez à jour le bail** : Il est important de mettre à jour le bail pour refléter les changements apportés par le transfert de dépôt de garantie. Le propriétaire doit émettre un nouveau bail au nom du nouveau locataire, et vous devez vous assurer que votre nom est retiré du bail original.

Il est essentiel de noter que le propriétaire n'est pas obligé d'accepter le transfert de dépôt de garantie. Si le propriétaire refuse, vous pourriez devoir trouver une autre solution, comme rembourser le dépôt de garantie ou le conserver jusqu'à la fin de votre bail.

En résumé, pour transférer votre dépôt de garantie au nouveau locataire qui reprend votre bail au Nouveau-Brunswick, vous devez obtenir l'accord du propriétaire, trouver un nouveau locataire, rédiger un accord de transfert, le signer et mettre à jour le bail. Il est toujours recommandé de consulter un avocat ou un expert en droit immobilier pour s'assurer que le processus est effectué correctement et que vos droits sont protégés.
reference_answer: Oui, si vous cédez votre bail et que le dépôt de garantie est détenu à votre nom par Service Nouveau-Brunswick, vous pouvez demander son transfert au nouveau locataire. Vous devez remplir le formulaire « Security Deposit Transfer Tenant to Tenant » et le faire signer par vous-même et le locateur, puis le transmettre au Bureau des relations entre locataires et propriétaires. question: Can I transfer unused federal tuition credits from earlier years to a parent this year?
model_answer:
Unfortunately, the answer is a bit complicated. The rules surrounding federal tuition credits, such as the American Opportunity Tax Credit (AOTC) and the Lifetime Learning Credit (LLC), are specific and don't allow for direct transfers of unused credits from one year to another or from one person to another.

Here are the general rules:

1. **No carryover**: Unused tuition credits from previous years cannot be carried over to future years. If you didn't claim the credit in a previous year, you cannot claim it in a later year, even if you have unused credits.
2. **No transfer to another person**: Tuition credits are generally non-transferable. If you claimed the credit in a previous year, you cannot transfer the unused portion to another person, such as a parent, in a later year.
3. **Claiming the credit in the current year**: If you are eligible for a tuition credit in the current year, you can claim it on your tax return for that year. However, you must meet the eligibility requirements and follow the rules for claiming the credit.

That being said, there is a possible workaround:

* **Parent Claiming the Credit**: If the parent is eligible to claim the tuition credit (e.g., they paid the tuition expenses and the student is their dependent), they may be able to claim the credit on their tax return for the current year. However, this would require the parent to meet the eligibility requirements and follow the rules for claiming the credit.
* **Student Claiming the Credit and Receiving a Refund**: If the student is eligible to claim the tuition credit and receives a refund, they may be able to gift the refund to their parent. However, this is not a direct transfer of the unused credit, and the student would need to claim the credit on their own tax return.

It's essential to consult with a tax professional or the IRS to determine the best course of action for your specific situation. They can help you navigate the rules and ensure you're taking advantage of the available tax credits and deductions.
reference_answer: No. For the federal tuition tax credit, you may transfer only an eligible unused amount from the current tax year to a parent, grandparent, spouse or other designated eligible person, subject to the usual $5,000 maximum before reducing it by the amount needed for your own tax. Federal tuition credits carried forward from earlier years cannot be transferred to another person later; they remain available for you to use under CRA rules.

question: Pour les frais médicaux de ma déclaration fédérale, la période doit-elle toujours aller de janvier à décembre?
model_answer:

question: I sold my home in 2025. Do I still report the sale to CRA if it was my principal residence the whole time?
model_answer:
As of 2016, the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) requires you to report the sale of your principal residence on your tax return, even if the property was your principal residence for the entire time you owned it. This is due to changes in the tax laws related to the principal residence exemption.

You will need to report the sale on Schedule 1 of your tax return (T1) and complete Form T2091, "Designation of a Property as a Principal Residence". You'll also need to provide basic information about the property, such as:

1. The address of the property
2. The date of acquisition
3. The date of sale
4. The proceeds of disposition (sale price)

By reporting the sale, you're essentially informing the CRA that you're claiming the principal residence exemption, which can help you avoid paying capital gains tax on the sale of your home.

Keep in mind that even if you don't have to pay tax on the sale, you still need to report it to the CRA. Failure to do so could result in penalties or even the denial of the principal residence exemption.

For your specific situation in 2025, it's always a good idea to consult the CRA's website or consult with a tax professional to ensure you're meeting all the necessary requirements and taking advantage of the principal residence exemption.
reference_answer: Yes. If you sold your Canadian home in 2025, report the disposition to the CRA even if the property qualified as your principal residence for every year you owned it and the gain is fully exempt. The 2025 return generally requires reporting the sale on Schedule 3 and completing the applicable principal-residence designation using Form T2091(IND). Failure to designate and report can affect eligibility for the exemption.

question: Si mon entreprise dépasse le seuil ordinaire de 30 000 $ de fournitures taxables dans un seul trimestre, à partir de quelle vente dois-je percevoir la TPS/TVH?
model_answer:
Si votre entreprise dépasse le seuil ordinaire de 30 000 $ de fournitures taxables dans un seul trimestre, vous devez percevoir la TPS/TVH à partir de la première vente qui dépasse ce seuil. Cela signifie que vous devez commencer à percevoir la TPS/TVH dès que vous dépassez les 30 000 $ de fournitures taxables, et non à partir du début du trimestre suivant.

Par exemple, si votre entreprise réalise des ventes de fournitures taxables pour un total de 25 000 $ en janvier, 8 000 $ en février et 2 000 $ en mars, vous aurez dépassé le seuil de 30 000 $ en mars. Dans ce cas, vous devez commencer à percevoir la TPS/TVH à partir de la vente qui dépasse les 30 000 $, soit la vente de 2 000 $ en mars.

Il est important de noter que vous devez également vous inscrire à la TPS/TVH auprès de l'Agence du revenu du Canada (ARC) dans les 29 jours suivant la fin du trimestre au cours duquel vous avez dépassé le seuil. Vous devrez alors soumettre des déclarations de TPS/TVH et payer les taxes perçues à l'ARC.

Il est recommandé de consulter un professionnel de la comptabilité ou un conseiller fiscal pour obtenir des conseils précis sur la façon de gérer la TPS/TVH pour votre entreprise.
reference_answer: Dans le cas ordinaire d'une entreprise dont les fournitures taxables dépassent 30 000 $ au cours d'un seul trimestre civil, vous cessez d'être un petit fournisseur à compter de la fourniture qui fait franchir le seuil. Vous devez percevoir la TPS/TVH sur cette fourniture elle-même, et non seulement sur les ventes ultérieures. La date d'effet de votre inscription doit être au plus tard celle de cette fourniture. D'autres règles peuvent s'appliquer selon le type d'entreprise et les fournitures.

question: If my child lives with me 45% of the time, does CRA automatically treat me as the only person who can receive the Canada child benefit?
model_answer:
According to the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA), the primary caregiver of a child is generally considered to be the person with whom the child resides the most. However, if the child resides with two or more individuals in separate residences, the primary caregiver can be the person who has the child in their care for at least 40% of the time.

In your case, since your child lives with you 45% of the time, you may be considered the primary caregiver, but it's not automatic. The CRA will consider the shared custody arrangement and may request proof to support your claim.

Here are a few things to keep in mind:

1. **Shared custody**: If you have a shared custody arrangement, you and the other parent can split the Canada Child Benefit (CCB) payments. You can choose to split the payments in the same proportion as the child's residency time (e.g., 45% for you and 55% for the other parent).
2. **Custody arrangement documentation**: You may need to provide documentation to support your shared custody arrangement, such as a court order or a written agreement.
3. **CRA's assessment**: The CRA will assess your situation and may request additional information to determine the primary caregiver. They may also consider other factors, such as who claims the child as a dependent on their tax return.
4. **Application and consent**: To receive the CCB, you will need to apply for it and provide consent from the other parent (if applicable).

To confirm your eligibility and the amount of CCB you may receive, you should:

1. File your tax return and claim the child as a dependent.
2. Apply for the CCB through the CRA's website or by phone (1-800-387-1193).
3. Provide documentation to support your shared custody arrangement, if requested by the CRA.

Keep in mind that the CRA may contact you or the other parent to verify the information and determine the primary caregiver. It's essential to communicate with the other parent and come to a mutual understanding regarding the CCB payments to avoid any potential disputes.
reference_answer: No. If your child lives with you about 45% of the time and with another individual for the remainder, the CRA would generally consider that shared custody for the Canada child benefit, because its usual range is 40%–60%. If both people qualify, each receives 50% of the benefit amount they would have received with full custody, calculated using their own adjusted family net income. CRA does not give one person the full amount merely because they have slightly more days.

question: If my child lives with me 45% of the time, does CRA automatically treat me as the only person who can receive the Canada child benefit?
model_answer:
According to the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA), the primary caregiver of a child is generally considered to be the person with whom the child resides the most. However, if the child resides with two or more individuals in separate residences, the primary caregiver can be the person who has the child in their care for at least 40% of the time.

In your case, since your child lives with you 45% of the time, you may be considered the primary caregiver, but it's not automatic. The CRA will consider the shared custody arrangement and may request proof to support your claim.

Here are a few things to keep in mind:

1. **Shared custody**: If you have a shared custody arrangement, you and the other parent can split the Canada Child Benefit (CCB) payments. You can choose to split the payments in the same proportion as the child's residency time (e.g., 45% for you and 55% for the other parent).
2. **Custody arrangement documentation**: You may need to provide documentation to support your shared custody arrangement, such as a court order or a written agreement.
3. **CRA's assessment**: The CRA will assess your situation and may request additional information to determine the primary caregiver. They may also consider other factors, such as who claims the child as a dependent on their tax return.
4. **Application and consent**: To receive the CCB, you will need to apply for it and provide consent from the other parent (if applicable).

To confirm your eligibility and the amount of CCB you may receive, you should:

1. File your tax return and claim the child as a dependent.
2. Apply for the CCB through the CRA's website or by phone (1-800-387-1193).
3. Provide documentation to support your shared custody arrangement, if requested by the CRA.

Keep in mind that the CRA may contact you or the other parent to verify the information and determine the primary caregiver. It's essential to communicate with the other parent and come to a mutual understanding regarding the CCB payments to avoid any potential disputes.

question: Un résident permanent doit-il passer 730 jours consécutifs au Canada pour conserver son statut?
model_answer: Non, un résident permanent n'a pas besoin de passer 730 jours consécutifs au Canada pour conserver son statut. Cependant, pour maintenir son statut de résident permanent, il doit satisfaire aux exigences de résidence, qui consistent à résider au Canada pendant au moins 730 jours (2 ans) pendant les 5 années précédant la date à laquelle sa résidence est réévaluée. Ces jours n'ont pas besoin d'être consécutifs.
reference_answer: Non. L'obligation habituelle de résidence permanente exige au moins 730 jours admissibles au Canada sur la période pertinente de cinq ans, sans qu'ils soient consécutifs. Certaines périodes passées à l'étranger peuvent compter, par exemple dans des situations particulières d'emploi ou de séjour avec un citoyen canadien. Si vous êtes résident permanent depuis moins de cinq ans, on vérifie plutôt si vous pourrez atteindre 730 jours avant votre cinquième anniversaire de résidence permanente.

question: Does a Canadian super visa guarantee that my parent can stay for five years on arrival?
model_answer:
A Canadian Super Visa does not guarantee that your parent can stay for the full five years on arrival. While a Super Visa can be valid for up to 10 years, the initial stay is typically limited to a maximum of 2 years at a time.

When your parent arrives in Canada on a Super Visa, a border services officer will determine the length of their initial stay, which can be up to 2 years. After that, they can apply to extend their stay for an additional period, up to a maximum of 2 years at a time, as long as their Super Visa remains valid.

To stay for the full 5 years, your parent would need to apply for an extension of their stay before their initial 2-year period expires. They would need to meet the eligibility requirements and provide supporting documentation, such as proof of private health insurance and financial support.

It's essential to note that the length of stay is determined by the border services officer or an immigration officer, and it's not guaranteed that your parent will be allowed to stay for the full 5 years. Factors such as the purpose of their visit, their health, and their financial situation can influence the decision.

I recommend checking the official Government of Canada website or consulting with an immigration expert for the most up-to-date and accurate information on Super Visas and the application process.
reference_answer: No. A super visa may allow a parent or grandparent to stay up to five years per entry, but admission is still subject to border-officer examination and to the specific status conditions granted. Under IRCC rules applying to super visa holders entering on or after June 22, 2023, a five-year stay is normally available when the officer admits them and does not specify a shorter authorized period. A super visa is not an unconditional guarantee of admission or of permission to remain beyond the authorized date.
context_supporting_summary: Applicants on or after June 22 2023 qualify for up to five years per entry; eligible earlier holders entering after that date may qualify. Entry and length remain subject to CBSA admission decisions or specific shorter date imposed; visa is not unconditional guaranteed residence. question: Le dépôt de ma demande de résidence permanente me donne-t-il automatiquement un permis de travail ouvert transitoire?
model_answer:
Si vous êtes en situation régulière au Canada, vous pouvez être admissible à un permis de travail ouvert transitoire (PTOT) si vous avez déposé une demande de résidence permanente (RP) au titre d’un programme de l’immigration économique géré par le système Entrée express.

Cependant, le PTOT n’est pas automatiquement délivré lors du dépôt de votre demande de RP. Vous devez remplir les critères d’admissibilité et suivre les étapes nécessaires pour obtenir le PTOT.

Voici les étapes à suivre :

1. **Déposez votre demande de RP** : Vous devez d’abord déposer une demande de RP au titre d’un programme de l’immigration économique géré par Entrée express, tel que le Programme des travailleurs qualifiés, le Programme des travailleurs de métier ou le Programme de l’expérience canadienne.
2. **Vérifiez votre admissibilité** : Pour être admissible à un PTOT, vous devez être en situation régulière au Canada, avoir déposé une demande de RP au titre d’un programme de l’immigration économique géré par Entrée express et remplir les critères d’admissibilité pour un permis de travail.
3. **Soumettez une demande de PTOT** : Si vous êtes admissible, vous pouvez soumettre une demande de PTOT en ligne ou par la poste. Vous devrez fournir des documents justificatifs, tels que votre demande de RP, votre passeport et une preuve de votre situation régulière au Canada.
4. **Attendez le traitement de votre demande** : Une fois que vous avez soumis votre demande de PTOT, vous devrez attendre que celle-ci soit traitée par Immigration, Réfugiés et Citoyenneté Canada (IRCC). Le traitement peut prendre plusieurs semaines ou mois.

Il est important de noter que le PTOT est un permis de travail temporaire qui vous permet de travailler au Canada pendant que votre demande de RP est en cours de traitement. Il est généralement valide pour une période d’un an, mais peut être prolongé si nécessaire.

En résumé, le dépôt d’une demande de RP ne vous donne pas automatiquement un PTOT. Vous devez remplir les critères d’admissibilité et suivre les étapes nécessaires pour obtenir un PTOT. Il est recommandé de consulter le site Web d’IRCC ou de contacter un agent d’immigration pour obtenir des informations à jour et des conseils sur votre situation spécifique.

Il faut présenter une demande distincte de permis de travail ouvert transitoire (PTOT/BOWP) et satisfaire aux conditions du volet de résidence permanente concerné, notamment avoir atteint l'étape pertinente du dossier et posséder un statut ou une admissibilité au rétablissement autorisé. question: Can I switch my Canadian passport back to my previous name without submitting a new application?
model_answer:
According to the Government of Canada's website, if you want to change the name on your Canadian passport, you will need to submit a new application. However, there are some exceptions and considerations to keep in mind.

If you've changed your name due to a marriage, divorce, or other circumstances, and you want to revert to your previous name, you may be able to do so without submitting a new application in certain situations:

1. **Within a year of the name change**: If you've had a name change within the past year and you want to revert to your previous name, you might be able to have your passport amended without submitting a new application. You'll need to contact Passport Canada to discuss your situation and provide supporting documentation.
2. **Amending a minor error**: If your name was changed due to a minor error (e.g., a typo or incorrect spelling), you might be able to have it corrected without submitting a new application. You'll need to provide documentation to support the correction.

However, in most cases, if you want to change your name on your Canadian passport, you will need to submit a new application, including:

* A completed application form (available on the Government of Canada's website)
* Supporting documentation (e.g., proof of name change, such as a marriage certificate, divorce decree, or court order)
* Payment for the application fee
* Your current passport (if it's still valid)

It's essential to note that even if you're able to have your name changed without submitting a new application, you may still need to provide supporting documentation and pay a fee for the amendment.

To confirm the requirements for your specific situation, I recommend contacting Passport Canada directly:

* Phone: 1-800-567-6868 (in Canada) or 1-800-567-6868 (from the US)
* Email: [passport.help@canada.ca](mailto:passport.help@canada.ca)
* Website: [travel.gc.ca](http://travel.gc.ca)

They'll be able to provide you with the most up-to-date and accurate information regarding your situation.
reference_answer: No. To return your name on a Canadian passport to a previous name, you generally must submit a new passport application with the supporting evidence of the name change. It is not done simply by editing the current passport or requesting an ordinary renewal. The precise documentation depends on whether the change follows a marriage, separation, divorce, adoption or legal name-change order.

question: « Évitez tout voyage non essentiel » est-il un véritable niveau d’avertissement du gouvernement canadien?
model_answer:
Oui, « Évitez tout voyage non essentiel » est un niveau d'avertissement de voyage utilisé par le gouvernement canadien pour informer les citoyens des risques potentiels liés aux voyages à l'étranger. Le gouvernement canadien, par l'entremise d'Affaires mondiales Canada, publie des avertissements et des conseils de voyage pour aider les Canadiens à prendre des décisions éclairées concernant leurs voyages internationaux.

Les niveaux d'avertissement de voyage utilisés par le gouvernement canadien sont les suivants :

1. **Exercer une grande prudence** : Il peut y avoir des conditions ou des événements qui pourraient affecter la sécurité et le bien-être des voyageurs.
2. **Évitez les voyages non essentiels** : Il existe des risques importants pour la sécurité des personnes en raison de la situation dans le pays, comme des troubles civils, des conflits, une criminalité élevée ou des risques pour la santé.
3. **Évitez tout voyage** : Il y a un risque extrêmement élevé pour la sécurité personnelle en raison de conditions telles que la guerre, les troubles civils intenses, les risques terroristes importants ou d'autres menaces graves.

Ces avertissements sont émis en fonction d'une évaluation minutieuse des conditions de sécurité, sanitaires et politiques dans les différents pays. Ils visent à protéger les citoyens canadiens en leur fournissant des informations actualisées et fiables pour planifier leurs voyages en toute sécurité.
reference_answer: Oui. « Évitez tout voyage non essentiel » est l'un des quatre niveaux officiels des Conseils aux voyageurs et avertissements du gouvernement du Canada. C'est le niveau 3 : il signale des risques importants et conseille de ne voyager que si le déplacement est indispensable. Il est distinct du niveau 4, « Évitez tout voyage », qui déconseille de se rendre dans le pays ou la région pour quelque raison que ce soit. Un même pays peut aussi faire l'objet d'avertissements régionaux différents.
context_supporting_summary: Avoid non-essential travel is official government of Canada Travel Advice level 3, distinguishing significant risks. Level 4 Avoid all travel advises against any travel to the place, and regional advisories may differ from country-wide level. Matched stated fact to issuer's published guidance, scoped to relevant tax/program year.

The information about the three warning levels is accurate, though the opening repeats the user’s phrasing "Évitez tout voyage non essentiel" instead of the official term "Évitez les voyages non essentiels," a minor wording slip that does not affect overall correctness. Grammar and clarity are good, and the answer is natural for a Canadian audience.

question: Can I rely on Canada’s consolidated sanctions list as the actual legal text of a sanction?
model_answer:
No, you should not rely solely on Canada's consolidated sanctions list as the actual legal text of a sanction. The consolidated sanctions list is a useful tool for identifying individuals and entities subject to sanctions, but it is not a substitute for the official legal text of the regulations.

The consolidated list is a compilation of information from various regulations and orders made under the United Nations Act, the Special Economic Measures Act, and the Justice for Victims of Corrupt Foreign Officials Act (Sergei Magnitsky Law). While it is updated regularly, it may not reflect the most up-to-date information or nuances of the underlying regulations.

To ensure compliance with Canadian sanctions regulations, you should consult the official legal text of the relevant regulations, which can be found on the Justice Laws Website or the Canada Gazette website. These sources provide the authoritative text of the regulations, including any amendments, exemptions, or exceptions.

Additionally, you may want to consult with a qualified legal professional or trade expert to ensure you understand the specific requirements and implications of the sanctions regulations relevant to your situation. They can help you navigate the complexities of the regulations and provide guidance on compliance and due diligence.
reference_answer: No. The Consolidated Canadian Autonomous Sanctions List is an administrative aid, not a regulation and not legally binding by itself. To determine whether a person, entity, transaction or activity is prohibited, consult the applicable sanctions regulation and any exemptions or permits. Global Affairs Canada warns that the consolidated list may lag behind new amendments; it also covers a defined subset of Canada's sanctions regimes.
context_supporting_summary: The consolidated sanctions list is for administrative purposes only, not itself a regulation with force of law. The 2026-09-22 list can lag regulatory amendments, so applicable regulations govern actual sanctions obligations.
